title: Beyond the Final Score: How Sports Became the New Investment Frontier
description: Discussion at the Sohn Investment Conference 2026 between investors Alexis Ohanian, Founder and General Partner, Seven Seven Six & Co-Founder and Former Executive Chairman, Reddit and Marc Lasry, Chairman, CEO and Co-Founder, Avenue Capital Group, moderated by Erik Serrano Berntsen, Chief Executive Officer, Stable. They discussed the transition of sports from trophy assets to institutional asset classes.
summary: The pitch argues that artificial intelligence threatens traditional entertainment sectors, leaving live sports as the final pillar of attention-grabbing content. Consequently, major streaming companies like Netflix, Google, and Amazon are expected to acquire sports teams or rights within the next 5 to 10 years to secure millions of viewers. The speaker posits that traditional sports will become increasingly valuable over the next decade specifically because they remain the last form of entertainment standing against AI disruption.

transcript: I'm Eric, founder and CEO of Stable, and I grew up in Madrid, which means I fully appreciate the power of sports. Every taxi I've ever gotten into anywhere in the world quickly agrees with me that Real Madrid is the best team on the planet. >> Ooh. >> So, normally I have a pretty smooth uh trip, and uh I'm very excited about this renewed Galacticos 3.0 uh era that's coming. So, like a football talent spotter, my job is to spot talent, but in the investment realm. So, what we do at Stable is we give new and up-and-coming fund managers lots of money, and we help them scale their firms. So, it's a pleasure here to be surrounded by two of the best players in the game. They've already proven that they can withstand the pressure of being in the arena. So, given it's a bit awkward to brag about yourself, I'm going to introduce them, and then we'll go into our sports investing masterclass. So, Alexis is the founder of 776, a venture firm that he started after co-founding Reddit. His uh investments read like a thesis statement of where the puck is going. I'm going to crassly try and fit in as many sports analogies as possible. He's a founding investor in Angel City Football Club, Chelsea Women's. Uh he's in golf, he's in volleyball. Um so, he's not just buying into leagues, he's actually building them. And one one fact I love about it is uh he first tweeted about this billion-dollar sports idea in 2019, and then he got dragged by millions of people on social media. Thanks for Reddit. It's been really helpful for the discourse. >> Yeah, I know. >> The good things also show up, though. Alex Morgan replied to you, I think, and that's how you got involved in ACFC. >> That's the reason I became the founding controller of Angel City. All All credit to Alex Morgan. >> So, good things happen from social media, too, then. It's good. >> Every now and then. >> Uh Mark, he's the co-founder, chairman, and CEO of Avenue. That's a lot of titles, Mark. I don't know how you find >> it's a lot of work. >> It's a lot of work, yeah. You got three three three jobs right there. He spent 40 years finding mispricings, and uh he's brought the same eye to sports. So, he invested in the Bucks, I think 2014, exit in '23. Is that right? >> Yes. >> Stake in North Carolina Courage, and you're a pickleball investor. Controversial. The good thing about Mark is that he's actually harvested returns as opposed to all these magical marks that we see in the market. And what's really interesting about Mark is I think he's good about discerning a market from a fad. Maybe except the pickleball, but we'll get there in a second. So just to set the table, why sports, why now? It's gone from trophy asset ego massage to institutional asset class in about 10 years. So let's start with Alexis. What made you allocate serious dollars to the space instead of it being a a passion bucket? >> Um you know, I laid it out in that tweet. I saw an opportunity in women's professional sports uh back in '19 simply because it was a World Cup Women's World Cup year. I didn't follow the sport, but I knew these stars had transcended it. That was a sign to me that there was something coming from spending 16 years building Reddit. I I'm like a heat-seeking missile for this kind of online engagement. And so the fact that Alex Morgan, Megan Rapinoe had millions and millions of followers told me that there was value there. And I'd seen a headline that Megan's team in Seattle had just sold for three, maybe three and a half million dollars. And the math didn't match for me. You know, I was like, "Well, look, she's worth at least that much money every year in brand deals. How is her team only worth that much? It must be really poorly run." And and I kind of went on this rant about how it was an obvious billion-dollar opportunity given, you know, the the sort of dearth in soccer excellence on the men's side here in this country. Um but the wealth of greatness that is on the women's. I know I can market greatness all day long. And and given this would be something very applicable, I think, to the women of the household who control all consumer spending, basically. It seemed like brands would sign up for it en masse. And uh you know, I I think for better or for worse, um my wife almost tried to talk me out of it. Uh so my wife is Serena Williams, and Serena and Venus are the case study for how women's sports, when invested in, can be just as valuable as men's, right? Because of Billie Jean King getting paid parity, because two girls in Compton saw the opportunity to make a ton of money playing sports, uh they became the greats and and blew up tennis, right? To this day, more Americans watch the US Open women's final than the men. And that is no discount to the men, but it's the fact that women's tennis is seen as just as valuable as men's, and the market says that. It's not activism or charity, it's it's the free market. And so that was my window into why it would work. And so far, off to a pretty good start. >> Thanks, Alexis. Mark, you've done it once already with the Bucks, and now you're buying in again. What's the thesis that keeps you coming back? >> Um well, I think part of it is you learn a lot by owning a team. Um and just, you know, for argument's sake, the pickleball investment, I bought it for 50,000, I sold it 2 years later for 5 billion. So, it actually worked. Um even though I never played it. But, I I think what you quickly learn in sports is um there's only three ways you make money. It's sort of uh ticket sales, sponsorship, and then media. The thing I loved about sports, and what I learned about the Bucks, and why you want to be invested in sports, is so your favorite team, I guess, is Real Madrid? >> Yep. >> All right. So, we'll use you as an example. If Real Madrid loses all their games, and they suck, you don't go and become a fan of Barcelona. >> No, never. >> Never. You're still going to be there. So, think about that. For all of you who have an iPhone or any product, normally, if a product like, here, we have a glass of water. If there was a hole in this glass, we would never use the glass, right? We'd throw it away. It's a bad product. Yet, Real Madrid could be horrible, and you don't switch. So, that what that taught me is that you have an asset that you could grow, and that every year you get more and more fans. Um so there is this sustainability to sports teams and to value and that value is what I I saw and I wanted to invest in. >> So you alluded to franchise versus ecosystem and those three verticals on how to make money. There's a real choice for capital on how to engage. Is it the franchise itself or we're also seeing opportunities in the ecosystem, hospitality, you know, real estate. Uh I wonder where are you putting your next dollar when you think about the vertical opportunity? >> So we invested in a company Cosm. I don't know if you've ever been there. Has anybody been there? >> Oh yeah. We got to watch the screen. >> it's the it's like these mini spheres and you go in and you feel you're sitting at the 50-yard line or you feel you're sitting courtside. And what So that's one of the verticals, but anything that is adjacent to sports people love. One of the things we quickly found out is um during COVID um you know, people wouldn't come into the office, right? You had remote and everybody worked remote. >> Mine still don't come in. >> Okay, so you're you're you're still working through >> Cracking the whip, cracking the >> Right? But people would go watch a Knicks game. People would go watch their teams and you'd be, you know, in the office everybody'd be like, "Oh, you got to be 6 ft away." But you'd then sit next somebody you didn't know and they would score and you'd go, "I love you!" >> Yes. >> Right? And you would touch and hug. So what you quickly found out is sports will transcend. And we love the verticals because um there is quite a bit of money that's going to be made there and we've invested in a number of those businesses. >> So let's talk about valuations and duration. Uh here we have sort of emerging to established life cycle. Alexis, when you're pricing a women's league or any new property, what does cheap even look like at this stage? >> I mean, you know, I can't talk about specific valuations, but like I recently bought the LA franchise for League 1 Volleyball. Um that's, you know, these valuations are all still let's say what would have been a normal seed round in venture capital, maybe not this year, uh but in prior years. And so I'm underwriting to, you know, building billion-dollar franchises. So, you know, at the end of the day I'm still looking to be on the ground floor. I can't say it was the first team in the league, uh but I I still want to be on the ground floor really helping to build, and I think where our expertise shines is on the operating from like zero to one. Mhm. Uh and so, you know, sub 100 million, let's say, valuation uh easily. >> Got it. And Mark, you watched the Bucks franchise, I don't know that's that's six, seven, eight X. I'm not very good at math, but pickleball sounds like a 100 X. It's pretty good. Um are we in fair value? Are we fairly priced for growth? Is it a bit frothy? What's the 60 seconds in your view on valuation now? >> I I I think everything is pretty fairly valued. I mean, ultimately what ends up happening is, you know, the problem with sports is if you want to make money, so you could buy a basketball team today, you'd make, I would say, 3 or 4%. So, that would be a decent return. But the problem ends up being that if you own a team, you want to win. And if you want to win, you spend money. So, that that's I I think that's the hard part in sports, and what we always see like Real Madrid, you want the team to win. You don't care if the owner makes money. You could you want him to spend as much as possible so they can win. And what ends up happening is you quickly realize that that when you own a team, your goal is to win. Yeah. And so, you build franchise value, and you build value the more you win, the more people want to end up owning that. So, when I sold the Bucks, I think we were losing a hundred million. And the reason for that is because we're in luxury tax. So, at the same time Michael Jordan was selling uh the Charlotte Hornets. >> Mhm. >> Hornets were selling and he sold them for three billion. They were making 50 million. The Bucks were losing a hundred million and we sold them for three and a half billion. >> Right. >> So, if I said to you, you want to What do you want? Three and a half billion you can lose a hundred or you want to make 15 and you can pay three billion? Why did somebody pay more? Because you're winning. Because your franchise value is greater. That's what you're doing day in day out in spending money. >> So, let's pull on that thread on how to win. Um Alexis, when you're thinking of yourself as an operator, you've obviously built a business. So, both of you wear these operator investor hats. >> Mhm. >> What value creation can you bring to the table to win more? Like, how do you think about adding value to the assets after you bought them? >> Oh, so I don't touch anything on the football side or the sporting side. Um I probably should offer more advice these days, especially with how much AI is just helping just revolutionize everyone when it comes to processing data, but that's not where my strengths are. So, I can't take any credit for even our our TGL team did win the championship this year. Can't take any credit for it, did nothing. I I just I I I where I think our leverage is is it ends up being maybe talent selection to some extent for the leadership on that side and I learned a lot of mistakes early on in sports uh that if I'd known Mark and asked him for advice sooner, maybe I could have avoided, but good lessons learned. Um and I think for value creation to me speaks to how do we use software in every part of our back office or I guess the front office um to actually run the business more efficiently. Once I got under the hood of sports teams and realized that most of the work happens on screen, happens in meetings, after meetings, making spreadsheets, collecting emails. Like, these are all things that software could do a hundred times more efficiently, especially now uh that software, you know, thanks to AI, is is truly commoditized. And so, all of our teams will always forevermore be run very asset-light, right? With a maybe a fraction of the people. I fully expect to have a front office with like, I don't know, maybe a dozen people max that are now managing agents to do things like outreach to, you know, the enterprise sales clients, social media content scaling massively through software instead of headcount. And I think those teams will just be run far more profitably than they were in the past. But I I on the football side or the sporting side, I not >> Mark, in your experience, that 100 million you were losing, I'm kind of interested in some anecdotes of where's the highest dollar to win conversion? Like, where would you spend that dollar to win? >> It's a great question. Cuz that was the big argument I would have with our GM. Is you know, when you understand math, you would say, "Well, why are we paying this person 20 million and this person 2 million? Is the guy you're paying 20 million 10 times better?" And the answer always is, "No, he's not. He's a little better." Well, they're like, "Okay, well, a little better means nothing." And so, what I ended up having the team focus on was we can figure out, yes, Giannis, you're going to give him the max, but your job is to find people who are 2 million who we can sign that are producing as if they're a 20 million-dollar player. And that's really hard. And that's what we really focused on. I would say the difference between Alexis and I is I would give our team pep talks, which didn't really do much. But I'm a big believer in pep talks. So, every time we'd have a game, I'm like, "Go out there and win." Um Put it in the basket. That's just an idea. >> I heard life, like football, is a game of inches. >> That's yes, that's And our golf team, I'd say guys hit it straight Uh and then when they didn't I was like see if you listened we would win but uh it's it's hard everyone's got to work hard Oh no they miss me oh yeah. >> So let's change gears a bit to all the investors in the room everyone's a bit stressed about liquidity all of us are adjusting our distribution winter models to see when we get any cash back from anything so what's this asset class actually worth when you sell you can you can you know market comparables on franchise value but the buyer universe is small the league approval gates everything I'm just curious maybe Alex is on the earlier stage things you own what's the path to liquidity are you thinking about exit? >> Yeah I mean look it's funny coming and I still do a lot of venture and a lot of tech like traditional tech and and it's funny I have seen investments in companies like Ripling or Flock or Row that are still a couple of years away from an IPO that I did in 2014 and so it's ironic like I actually can see it you know we talk about the illiquidity of sports historically but even tech obviously is dealing with its own challenges around it where there was sort of always a traditional path to IPO and it still it will come but I think this tidal wave of investment that's now opened up private equity is obviously investing in a big way in sports it's not just a trophy asset for billionaires and you know three years ago when DALL-E dropped that was the first image generation tool for open AI I'm out here playing with it posting my little images and they're janky but but good and I was on stage not too much longer saying okay guys so images happen way faster than I expected than a lot of us in tech expected videos are just moving images so I've got a line of sight to probably the next couple of years seeing some really incredible video generation like text to image and then text to video when that happens there will be an existential crisis in Hollywood because so many of the biggest budget films were all just guys in green tights and gals in green tights in front of green screens. When you can reproduce that budget for a fraction of the cost, and if you've seen any of the new seed dance models on your Twitter feed, you see what I'm talking about. Those things all lined up. And very quickly, one of the pillars of entertainment is going to be under existential threat because of AI. So, let's look to the next one, music industry. Same thing. And again, all this stuff you can see it on my Twitter like 2 and 1/2 years ago. You'll have one-hit will have a chart-topping songs that are entirely AI-generated. Sho- They're here. They're already here. And and live events will still matter. That will be I'm still taking my daughter to see Taylor Swift in 10 years. But a bunch of one-hit wonders will be never again, and instead, AI will generate that because this tech is that good. But what's left is sports. And the guarantee was when you need to capture millions of people to tune in when the stakes have to be there and live and real, sports will be the last one left standing because even when you have robots, no one wants to watch a bunch of European robots face off a bunch of American robots in a game of 18 hole-in-ones of golf. All right, that is not entertaining. There will be robots fighting each other, that will be a thing, sort of BattleBots but with humanoid robots, but set that aside. Traditional sports will actually be even more valuable as a way to capture attention 10 years from now. And if I am one of the companies left standing in the business of trying to capture people's attention, the obvious ones are the streamers. So, whether it's Google, Amazon, Netflix, you're already seeing it, right? Netflix created content of a guy climbing a building, and millions of people tuned in for it, and it's not I mean, it is a sport, but it's not a traditional sport in the sense, but it it's a glimpse into the future. And so, I think there are exits that abound for emerging leagues to some of the big streaming companies that in the next 5 to 10 years will absolutely need to find the last thing left that they can guarantee millions of people will tune in for. It's sports. And and then for the teams themselves, I think again, I think the sky's the limit as people realize that to Mark's point, the tattoo test, when I knew Reddit, I knew Reddit would be successful 3 years in because I met the first Redditor who tattooed the logo, the little alien that I created, on their body. And it was weird. His name is Fernando Takai. I actually checked in with him recently. He did get the tattoo removed. Um Sorry, Fernando. >> technology. That's a tip you've heard here today. That's going to be a >> But the reason why I thought it was I knew we'd be successful is because if you can create a brand that someone is willing to tattoo on their body in just 3 years, like we're onto something very special. And very few corporate brands ever reach the point where they get tattooed on people's bodies, right? Maybe the Nike swoosh, some Disney Marvel IP, Playboy Bunny. There's a few, right? But sports, every one of those are corporate logos. And we take for granted the fact that people There's probably a few people here have Knicks tattoos right now, right? Sports logos are taken for granted as things that we tattoo on our bodies forever. And so the power of brand that these institutions have is so significant and still so undervalued in a world where we will be full of more and more AI slop, and and these are the things that can actually break through. So I'm not worried. I think there will be plenty of exit opportunities over the next 10 years. >> Good to hear that we're all going to get our money back. So we have a 30 seconds left. I've got a final question for each of you. What sport doesn't belong in an institutional portfolio yet, but is something that you're looking to add in the next few years? >> Padel. >> Padel? >> That's a good one. >> That's a good one. >> I don't want to give away all the alpha. If I I got to buy a team in the things first. >> paying to be here for charity. They need something. >> Yeah, okay. All right, fair enough. I um Well, you know, okay, one of the lessons from NWSL is I should have bought the league instead of just started a team. And so I set my sights on the Olympics, and one of the most popular sports there every 4 years is track and field. So I ended up starting a league called Athlos. I think I think there will be other opportunities in Olympic sports that are extremely popular every 4 years and then disappear. We just have to figure out how to build a community around that. So, you can go through the list, you can find them. >> Curling. Curling would >> Uh, well >> Huge. >> Huge. >> Maybe gymnastics, you know, maybe swimming. I don't know about curling, but >> Curling. >> There's probably some big curling fans out there. >> going to invest in this. >> Get a broom, a broom sponsor. >> Curling. >> I mean, you know, but think about that. Here's a sport. Somebody says to you here's what I'm going to do. I'm going to roll a ball. I'm going to roll it on ice. >> Well, it's a puck. It's a giant puck. And you shove it >> I'm going to have one guy with a little >> Sweeping. Yeah. >> Like this. That guy's got to really do it hard. >> In this Olympics, the first time we heard heard a Canadian swear. That was a big >> I know. >> Yeah, that's crazy. >> Unfortunately, that's all the time the clock will give us. Alexis, Mark, thank you. >> Pleasure. >> Thank you.
